network.overall_strategy: This is an evidence-graded, connected synthesis network with exactly 10 pathway entries, not 10 independently validated de novo mechanisms. It combines discharge/Strecker chemistry, experimentally reported but mechanistically unresolved acetone/cyanide and heated-formaldehyde chemistry, reduced-gas shock chemistry, three experimentally tested metal-catalyst variants of alpha-ketoisovalerate reductive amination, and three explicitly speculative substrate-scope extensions. P5-P7 are catalyst variants, not different carbon-skeleton construction mechanisms. Alpha-ketoisovalerate is an explicitly supplied starting precursor: the cited research does not establish its prebiotic synthesis from simpler feedstocks. Discharge production of the required branched aldehyde is also insufficiently characterized. Consequently, experimentally demonstrated closure of the entire network from simple geochemical feedstocks cannot be claimed. Empirical process nodes collapse unresolved chemistry rather than inventing molecular identities for heterogeneous precursor material; the carbon dioxide closure proposed for rxn_006 and rxn_007 is explicitly hypothetical. Environments represent separate reaction settings, not a single compatible vessel. Shock and discharge involve transient energetic events outside ordinary bulk-water temperature ranges. All chemistry is anoxic; sulfite and ferrous hydroxide supply reducing equivalents without molecular oxygen. Organic formulas use neutral reference structures, with acid-base speciation described in conditions. Valine is stereochemically unspecified and expected to be racemic absent demonstrated symmetry breaking. A null environment_formed denotes an imported feedstock or formation in multiple environments. Byproducts use the allowed intermediate role.

reactions.name: Reduced-gas discharge supplying cyanide and a candidate branched aldehyde

conditions.temperature: 300-330 K collection water; much hotter transient electrical-discharge channels
conditions.pressure: approximately 1 atm in a proposed local gas-water setting
conditions.other: Anoxic methane/ammonia-rich gas over water; repeated electrical discharge and aqueous collection. The listed products are a selected-product projection of a much broader mixture.

reactions.mechanism: Discharge-driven fragmentation and recombination generate hydrogen cyanide and carbonyl compounds. Formation of 2-methylpropanal is a proposed branched-carbon component of this unresolved upstream network, not an established elementary sequence.
reactions.reasoning: Miller (1957) established discharge production of HCN and aldehydes and their connection to Strecker synthesis; Ring et al. (1972) directly identified valine in a related discharge product mixture. The supplied findings do not establish a measured, isotope-resolved discharge-to-isobutyraldehyde sequence, so that species-specific edge is speculative. Producing sufficient branched C4 aldehyde is the key skeleton bottleneck. A locally reducing mixture is required; a globally persistent methane/ammonia atmosphere is not assumed, given Trail et al. (2011). No mineral catalyst is justified.

reactions.name: Isobutyraldehyde-ammonia condensation

conditions.other: Concentrated, mildly alkaline water, approximately pH 8-9; imine is a transient equilibrium intermediate. Rapid cyanide capture must compete with hydrolysis and aldehyde loss.

reactions.mechanism: Ammonia adds to the aldehyde, followed by carbinolamine dehydration to an imine. Subsequent cyanide addition can pull the reversible condensation forward.
reactions.reasoning: This is the conventional Strecker condensation underlying the mechanistic framework of Miller (1957). Its application to isobutyraldehyde is chemically well motivated, but the cited findings do not separately quantify this imine or its equilibrium abundance. Concentration and capture, rather than an unjustified mineral catalyst, are the relevant controls.

reactions.name: Cyanide addition forming valine aminonitrile

conditions.other: Approximately pH 8-9, with HCN/CN- and imine/iminium speciation. Water depth or pore shading reduces photodestruction without requiring an ozone layer.

reactions.mechanism: Cyanide attacks the imine/iminium carbon. Proton transfer gives 2-amino-3-methylbutanenitrile; cyanide supplies the future carboxyl carbon.
reactions.reasoning: Miller (1957) supports aminonitrile formation as the central Strecker intermediate, while Ring et al. (1972) supports accessibility of valine in discharge chemistry. This carbon addition gives the correct C5 connectivity, unlike ordinary acetone Strecker chemistry, which gives alpha-aminoisobutyric acid. Valine-specific rates and competing cyanide reactions remain insufficiently characterized.

reactions.name: Valine aminonitrile hydration to valinamide

conditions.other: Proposed acidification to approximately pH 1-3 after cyanide capture, for example in an acidic geothermal pool. Required residence time is not established for this substrate.

reactions.mechanism: Nitrile protonation, water addition and proton transfers produce the corresponding primary amide.
reactions.reasoning: Miller (1957) supports aminonitrile hydrolysis as the source of accumulated amino acids. The explicit valinamide node and these mildly heated environmental conditions are a mechanistic reconstruction, not a separately reported valine-specific experiment. Strong analytical acid hydrolysis should not be equated with rapid natural hydrolysis; this step requires kinetic validation.

reactions.name: Valinamide hydrolysis to valine

conditions.other: Approximately pH 1-3 following rxn_004; released ammonia is predominantly ammonium. Residence time and product survival require measurement.

reactions.mechanism: Water addition to the protonated amide carbonyl and C-N bond cleavage release valine and ammonia/ammonium.
reactions.reasoning: This completes the conventional nitrile-to-amino-acid chemistry supported at the reaction-family level by Miller (1957). Separate valinamide kinetics under the proposed surface conditions are not supplied, so this step is an explicit mechanistic extrapolation. Hydrolysis may be a bottleneck, and the reported analytical recovery of amino acids does not establish efficient free-valine accumulation in every natural pool.

reactions.name: Acetone-ammonium-cyanide valine production: empirical process with hypothetical coproduct closure

conditions.temperature: 300-350 K proposed accumulation stage; subsequent hydrolysis conditions are not established by the supplied summary
conditions.other: Concentrated cyanide/ammonia pool containing acetone, followed by hydrolytic processing. This is not a validated single-temperature natural protocol.

reactions.mechanism: An unresolved cyanide/ketone network constructs additional C-C bonds and produces valine or hydrolysable valine precursors. The graph proposes internal redox disproportionation with CO2 and regenerated ammonia as an atom-balance-compatible closure; those coproduct assignments are not experimentally established.
reactions.reasoning: Friedmann and Miller (1969) directly obtained valine when acetone was added to NH4CN, but failed to confirm valine from NH4CN alone. Ordinary acetone Strecker chemistry cannot explain this result because it yields a C4 amino acid. Valine production is supported; the detailed branching mechanism, natural hydrolysis conditions and the CO2-containing closure represented here are speculative. Stoichiometric inference from this node must not be treated as an experimentally measured yield or carbon map.

reactions.name: Heated formaldehyde-ammonia chemistry: historical empirical valine branch

conditions.temperature: approximately 458 K heating stage, followed by cooling and hydrolytic processing
conditions.pressure: greater than approximately 12 bar if liquid water is retained; proposed confined-pore analogue
conditions.other: Concentrated formaldehyde/ammonia chemistry. Hydrothermal placement is an environmental extrapolation, not a claim that the original experiment reproduced a vent. Hydrolysis work-up requirements remain a separate uncertainty.

reactions.mechanism: Thermal carbonyl condensation, nitrogen incorporation and internal redox chemistry form complex hydrolysable products. The valine-specific branched sequence is unresolved. CO2 is proposed as an oxidized coproduct permitting formal carbon/redox closure, not as an experimentally traced valine-associated product.
reactions.reasoning: Fox and Windsor (1970) historically reported valine after heating formaldehyde/ammonia products and hydrolysing them. However, Kebukawa et al. (2017) considered L-only valine in a related thermal system likely contamination. This is therefore a low-confidence empirical branch, not a reproducibly quantified modern synthesis. The CO2 coproduct assignment and transfer to a confined terrestrial hydrothermal setting are speculative and require isotopic validation.

reactions.name: Reduced-gas shock, rapid quench and aqueous recovery of valine

conditions.temperature: Transient high-temperature shock, followed by rapid cooling into approximately 300-330 K collection water
conditions.pressure: transient shock compression followed by decompression; no specific pressure inferred from the supplied summary
conditions.other: Gas-phase initiation using approximately 3.3% methane, 11% ethane and 5.6% ammonia in argon. Water enters subsequent collection/hydrolysis, not the initial reduced-gas shock. This is a surface event, not an isothermal 300-370 K pool reaction.

reactions.mechanism: Shock-induced fragmentation and radical recombination create reduced nitrogenous organic products. Rapid quenching preserves reactive intermediates; aqueous processing supplies oxygen and can release amino acids. The listed outputs are a selected-product projection, not a resolved elementary mechanism.
reactions.reasoning: Bar-Nun et al. (1970) directly reported valine from this reduced-gas shock family. The valine-specific intermediate sequence and product-associated hydrogen stoichiometry were not resolved. Its environmental limitation is the highly reduced starting gas, given Trail et al. (2011). Takeuchi et al. (2020) demonstrated amino-acid formation in more conservative CO2/N2/Fe impact mixtures but did not demonstrate valine, so those experiments cannot close this feedstock gap.

reactions.name: Nickel-catalysed reductive amination of alpha-ketoisovalerate

conditions.catalyst: Ni/SiO2-Al2O3; 10 mol% Ni relative to ketoacid
conditions.other: 30 mM alpha-ketoisovalerate, five equivalents NH4HCO3, pH approximately 8, 72 hours. This is a cool pressurized aqueous interface, not a hot vent interior.

reactions.mechanism: Ammonia forms an imine/iminium-type intermediate at the alpha-keto group. Nickel activates hydrogen and hydrogenates that intermediate to valine.
reactions.reasoning: Kaur et al. (2024) directly tested alpha-ketoisovalerate. Their approximately 20% combined amino/hydroxy-acid yield and 34:66 product ratio imply about 6.8% valine, an arithmetic inference rather than a separately reported yield. Catalyst-free controls lacked reduction products. Hydrogen and nickel have plausible geological sources, but the supported catalyst is a laboratory material and the 30 mM branched ketoacid was supplied, not synthesized in the network.

reactions.name: Palladium-catalysed reductive amination benchmark

conditions.catalyst: Pd/C; 1 mol% Pd relative to ketoacid
conditions.other: 30 mM alpha-ketoisovalerate, five equivalents NH4HCO3, pH approximately 8, 72 hours.

reactions.mechanism: Palladium-mediated hydrogen activation reduces the ammonia-derived imine/iminium intermediate to valine.
reactions.reasoning: Kaur et al. (2024) directly reported approximately 77% combined amino/hydroxy-acid yield with an 83:17 ratio, implying about 64% valine. This is the most selective of the three tested catalyst variants but is retained as an experimental benchmark, not asserted to be an abundant prebiotic catalyst. Natural availability of comparably active palladium surfaces and the origin of alpha-ketoisovalerate remain unresolved.

reactions.name: Meteoritic Fe-Ni-catalysed reductive amination
agents: ground Aletai iron meteorite containing nickel-bearing metallic phases

conditions.catalyst: 3 mg ground Aletai meteorite in the reported experiment
conditions.other: 30 mM alpha-ketoisovalerate, five equivalents NH4HCO3, pH approximately 8, 72 hours. Activity of weathered natural surfaces is not established.

reactions.mechanism: Hydrogen activation and imine hydrogenation occur on reactive meteoritic metal surfaces; competing ketone hydrogenation diverts substrate to the hydroxy acid.
reactions.reasoning: Kaur et al. (2024) directly reported approximately 74% combined amino/hydroxy-acid yield and an 18:82 ratio, implying about 13% valine. Meteorite-derived metal is a more directly natural material than Pd/C, but hydroxy-acid formation dominates. The experiment does not demonstrate formation of the branched ketoacid or preservation of activity after terrestrial surface alteration.

reactions.name: Competing hydrogenation of alpha-ketoisovalerate to its hydroxy acid
agents: ground Aletai meteorite as one tested alternative

conditions.catalyst: One of the three listed catalysts, used separately rather than mixed
conditions.other: Same aqueous ketoacid/ammonium conditions as rxn_009-rxn_011; catalyst-dependent competition with reductive amination.

reactions.mechanism: Surface-mediated hydrogenation of the keto carbonyl produces 2-hydroxy-3-methylbutanoic acid instead of forming a C-N bond.
reactions.reasoning: Kaur et al. (2024) directly measured this competing product. Its shares of the combined amino/hydroxy products were approximately 66% for supported Ni, 17% for Pd/C and 82% for Aletai meteorite. This terminal side branch is included because a valine network that ignores the dominant carbon sink on geochemically attractive catalysts would overstate productivity; no unsupported conversion of this hydroxy acid back to valine is added.

reactions.name: Hypothetical alpha-ketoisovalerate Bucherer-Bergs conversion to hydantoin

conditions.temperature: approximately 300 K proposed surface analogue of the reported room-temperature stage
conditions.other: Reaction-class benchmark: approximately 0.35 M ketoacid, 1.2 equivalents cyanide, two equivalents ammonia source and 0.5 M bicarbonate at pH approximately 8.5 for 21 days. These are not established optimal valine conditions. CO2 appears on both sides to represent inorganic-carbon exchange in the lumped process.

reactions.mechanism: Proposed cyanide/ammonia addition, inorganic-carbon capture, cyclization and decarboxylative processing yield 5-isopropylhydantoin. The intervening carboxylated species and carbon-atom mapping are not assigned as experimentally established valine intermediates.
reactions.reasoning: SPECULATIVE substrate extension. Pulletikurti et al. (2022) established alpha-ketoacid-to-amino-acid chemistry involving hydantoins, but did not directly demonstrate alpha-ketoisovalerate-to-valine in the documented substrate set. This proposed step is justified by the shared alpha-ketoacid functionality, not by a valine experiment. Precursor supply, concentrated bicarbonate/cyanide, branching-dependent kinetics and the exact decarboxylation sequence remain unresolved.

reactions.name: Hypothetical hydrolytic opening of valine hydantoin

conditions.other: Warm bicarbonate/ammonia solution following rxn_013. Fourteen days is the reported reaction-class heated-stage duration, not a measured lifetime for this specific hydantoin.

reactions.mechanism: Hydrolytic cleavage of the hydantoin ring produces N-carbamoylvaline.
reactions.reasoning: SPECULATIVE valine-specific extension. Pulletikurti et al. (2022) provided mechanistic support for hydantoin hydrolysis through N-carbamoyl amino acids. The proposed isopropyl-substituted substrate was not directly validated in the supplied findings. Slow ring opening, competing degradation and dependence on ammonia-source chemistry must be tested rather than inferred from the generic temperature protocol.

reactions.name: Hypothetical N-carbamoylvaline hydrolysis

conditions.other: Continuation of the heated hydrolysis stage; ammonia/ammonium and CO2/bicarbonate speciation depend on pH. No separate valine-specific completion time is asserted.

reactions.mechanism: Hydrolytic removal of the carbamoyl group releases valine, ammonia and inorganic carbon.
reactions.reasoning: SPECULATIVE valine-specific extension of the N-carbamoyl-amino-acid chemistry described by Pulletikurti et al. (2022). This is a chemically justified deprotection step, but its rate and yield for N-carbamoylvaline under the proposed conditions are unestablished. Merely reaching a hydantoin or carbamoylated precursor must not be counted as demonstrated accumulation of free valine.

reactions.name: Hypothetical ferrous-hydroxide-driven reductive amination
agents: freshly precipitated iron(II) hydroxide, consumed as a reductant rather than acting as a conserved catalyst

conditions.pressure: sufficient hydrostatic pressure to retain liquid water
conditions.other: Approximately pH 8.8-9.3, low ionic strength and fresh reactive Fe(II) hydroxide. Ferric oxyhydroxide is a proposed oxidized end phase, not an established phase assignment for this valine reaction.

reactions.mechanism: Ammonia-derived imine formation is followed by electron transfer coupled to oxidation of Fe(II). The displayed formal net reaction uses FeOOH to close the two-electron reduction without molecular oxygen.
reactions.reasoning: SPECULATIVE substrate and solid-product extension. Huber and Wachtershauser (2003) demonstrated reductive amination of other alpha-ketoacids with freshly prepared FeS or Fe(OH)2, not alpha-ketoisovalerate. Fe(OH)2 is represented as a consumed electron donor to avoid inventing a reductant-free catalytic cycle. The actual oxidized solid could be mixed-valence or poorly crystalline rather than the displayed FeOOH reference phase. Salinity, aging and carbonate precipitation may suppress the proposed chemistry.

reactions.name: Hypothetical ZnS-photocatalysed valine formation with sulfite oxidation

conditions.other: Anoxic suspension at approximately pH 9. Sulfite is a consumed hole scavenger/electron donor, not a catalyst. Natural UV spectrum, mineral defects and surface aging require separate evaluation.

reactions.mechanism: UV excitation generates electron-hole pairs. Photogenerated reducing equivalents reduce an ammonia-derived imine, while sulfite scavenges oxidizing equivalents. Sulfate represents the proposed fully oxidized sulfur endpoint; water cancels in the formal net reaction.
reactions.reasoning: SPECULATIVE valine-specific extension. Wang et al. (2012) demonstrated ZnS-driven photochemical amination of other alpha-ketoacids, with improved performance when sulfite scavenged holes, but did not test alpha-ketoisovalerate. The shared carbonyl chemistry motivates this experiment; it does not establish a valine yield. Sulfur-product distribution, substrate photodegradation, competition with hydroxy-acid formation and natural-sunlight efficiency remain open questions.

pathways.name: Reduced-gas discharge followed by explicit Strecker chemistry
pathways.description: Methane/ammonia/water processing supplies cyanide and a hypothesized branched aldehyde; imine formation, cyanide capture and sequential hydrolysis yield valine. Direct discharge valine evidence exists, but branched-aldehyde production and natural hydrolysis kinetics are incompletely resolved.

pathways.name: Acetone plus discharge-supplied cyanide
pathways.description: Discharge supplies HCN to an acetone/ammonia pool. Valine production has direct historical support, but the intervening C-C chemistry and displayed coproduct closure remain unresolved. This is not ordinary acetone Strecker chemistry and does not claim valine from cyanide alone.

pathways.name: Thermal formaldehyde-ammonia empirical route
pathways.description: Heated C1 carbonyl/ammonia chemistry followed by hydrolytic processing is represented as one unresolved process. Historical valine detection is qualified by later contamination concerns and by uncertainty about a natural hydrolysis protocol.

pathways.name: Reduced-gas shock and aqueous recovery
pathways.description: Methane, ethane and ammonia undergo shock processing, rapid quenching and aqueous recovery. This has direct product-level evidence but requires an unusually reduced local gas mixture and a transient event outside ordinary surface-pool thermal conditions.

pathways.name: Supported-nickel hydrogenation of supplied alpha-ketoisovalerate
pathways.description: Experimentally demonstrated final-step valine synthesis using Ni and hydrogen. Conditional on an external branched ketoacid supply; it does not solve carbon-skeleton formation. Competing hydroxy-acid production is represented by rxn_012.

pathways.name: Palladium benchmark for supplied alpha-ketoisovalerate
pathways.description: A directly tested, comparatively selective catalyst variant of P5, not a separate carbon-skeleton pathway. Palladium availability and an external alpha-ketoisovalerate supply limit its geochemical interpretation.

pathways.name: Meteoritic-metal hydrogenation of supplied alpha-ketoisovalerate
pathways.description: A directly tested natural-material catalyst variant using ground Aletai meteorite. The supplied ketoacid requirement and dominant hydroxy-acid sink remain substantial limitations.

pathways.name: Conditional ketoacid Bucherer-Bergs pathway
pathways.description: Discharge-derived cyanide reacts with supplied alpha-ketoisovalerate, ammonia and inorganic carbon to form a proposed hydantoin, followed by ring opening and decarbamoylation. All valine-specific transformations in this pathway are substrate-scope hypotheses rather than direct demonstrations.

pathways.name: Conditional ferrous-hydroxide reductive amination
pathways.description: Fresh Fe(II) hydroxide is proposed to supply reducing equivalents for amination of externally supplied alpha-ketoisovalerate. Both the valine substrate extension and the specific oxidized iron end phase require experimental validation.

pathways.name: Conditional ZnS/sulfite photochemical amination
pathways.description: UV-illuminated ZnS and consumed sulfite are proposed to convert externally supplied alpha-ketoisovalerate into valine. This extends an established alpha-ketoacid reaction class but is not a reported valine experiment.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The identified aldehyde, imine, aminonitrile and amide form a chemically coherent Strecker route to valine. Miller (1957) supports the general mechanism, and Ring et al. (1972) directly demonstrated discharge-derived valine. However, those findings do not establish the specific isobutyraldehyde output or product proportions represented by rxn_001. Its conservation balance does not resolve that evidential gap. A transient discharge is compatible with a surface setting, but aqueous capture and hydrolysis conditions are not specified sufficiently to establish end-to-end operation.
suggestions: Quantify isobutyraldehyde production and capture under the actual discharge conditions; distinguish this uncertainty from the better-established production of HCN.
Specify pH, temperature, residence time and aqueous trapping conditions for rxn_002 through rxn_005.
Measure competition from other carbonyl compounds and attach Miller (1957) and Ring et al. (1972) to the appropriate reaction records.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Friedmann and Miller (1969) directly support valine formation from acetone plus ammonium cyanide, so retaining an empirical process node is reasonable. This must not be interpreted as ordinary acetone Strecker chemistry, which gives alpha-aminoisobutyric acid rather than valine. The proposed CO2 coproduct closure is not experimentally established. P2 uses the relatively well-supported HCN output of rxn_001 and does not require its uncertain isobutyraldehyde output, although the shared reaction node remains incompletely characterized.
suggestions: Specify cyanide and ammonia concentrations, incubation conditions, and the analytical hydrolysis or recovery procedure used to establish valine production.
Retain rxn_006 as a process-level observation and distinguish inferred balancing coefficients from measured reactant consumption and coproduct yields.
Use isotope tracing and coproduct analysis to test the additional carbon-carbon chemistry and proposed CO2 production.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Fox and Windsor (1970) provide historical product-level support, but this is not a resolved direct conversion of formaldehyde and ammonia into free valine. Amino acids were recovered after hydrolysis of complex material. The hypothetical CO2 closure does not establish the branched-carbon mechanism or actual product distribution. Kebukawa et al. (2017) identified apparent valine in a related thermal system as probable contamination; the differing recipe prevents treating that result as a direct refutation, but it substantially limits confidence in generalization. A hydrothermal label alone does not specify the required heating and work-up.
suggestions: Define the empirical process boundary to include thermal precursor formation and subsequent hydrolysis, without inventing structures for heterogeneous material.
Specify the approximately 185 degrees Celsius heating protocol, duration, pressure or phase state, and separate recovery conditions.
Seek modern isotope-labeled replication with procedural blanks, orthogonal product identification and enantiomer analysis.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Bar-Nun et al. (1970) directly demonstrated valine formation from reduced gases subjected to shock heating and rapid quenching. Representing this as an empirical process is defensible, provided the arrow includes the appropriate aqueous recovery rather than implying that free valine survives at peak shock temperature. The supplied conservation check supports the formal equation, not its inferred product proportions. The surface designation is not intrinsically inconsistent with a transient shock, but pulse conditions, quench kinetics and gas availability remain unspecified.
suggestions: Specify gas composition, inert diluent, shock temperature and pressure, pulse duration, cooling rate and aqueous recovery procedure.
Distinguish measured amino-acid production from the hypothetical net H2 yield and other uncharacterized products.
If making a geological claim, justify a local or transient reduced-gas reservoir rather than assuming a persistent global atmosphere.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Kaur et al. (2024) directly support nickel-catalyzed conversion of supplied alpha-ketoisovalerate to valine. The declared starting precursor makes this a valid one-step synthesis without requiring an upstream carbon-skeleton construction route. The competing hydroxy-acid branch is appropriately included: the reported 20% combined yield and 34:66 amino-to-hydroxy ratio imply approximately 6.8% valine, not 20%. Environmental confidence is limited by the absence of an explicit operating recipe and justification of the active supported-nickel material. rxn_012 is evaluated as a competing branch, not a second productive step.
suggestions: Specify the demonstrated conditions: 30 mM ketoacid, five equivalents NH4HCO3, pH 8, 5 bar H2, 22 degrees Celsius, 72 hours and supported catalyst containing 10 mol% Ni relative to substrate.
Track valine and hydroxy-acid yields separately and quantify additional carbon losses.
Distinguish the tested supported catalyst from untested natural nickel phases, and retain the supplied-precursor scope limitation.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This is the strongest demonstrated productive branch for the stated feedstocks. Kaur et al. (2024) reported a 77% combined valine-plus-hydroxy-acid yield with an 83:17 product ratio, implying approximately 64% valine. The reductive-amination mechanism and final product are well supported. Calling Pd/C a benchmark appropriately avoids claiming that its laboratory performance establishes natural availability. The generic environment label still needs an explicit recipe. Selection as the best pathway reflects experimental evidence and selectivity, not a preference for palladium or for a particular precursor framework.
suggestions: Specify the Kaur et al. conditions and Pd/C loading containing 1 mol% Pd relative to substrate.
Report the approximately 64% inferred valine yield separately from the 77% combined product yield.
Maintain the laboratory-benchmark designation; substantiate active catalyst availability separately if extending the claim to a natural setting.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Kaur et al. (2024) directly demonstrated valine formation using ground Aletai meteorite. The reported 74% combined yield and 18:82 amino-to-hydroxy ratio imply approximately 13% valine, with hydroxy-acid formation dominating. This is strong evidence for the final conversion, but not proof that arbitrary Fe-Ni minerals or weathered meteorites have equivalent activity. Imported alpha-ketoisovalerate is a valid boundary condition. The missing operating details and catalyst surface-state specification prevent stronger environmental confidence.
suggestions: Specify the tested meteorite identity, composition, grinding or surface preparation, 3 mg loading, and corresponding solution and H2 conditions.
Quantify hydroxy-acid diversion explicitly rather than equating total substrate reduction with valine production.
Test catalyst aging and passivation before extrapolating from freshly ground Aletai material to a natural exposure.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Interpreted as rxn_001 supplying HCN followed by rxn_013 through rxn_015, this matches the stated four-step pathway. Pulletikurti et al. (2022) support the reaction class and hydantoin/N-carbamoyl sequence, but not alpha-ketoisovalerate-to-valine specifically. The proposed intermediate identities are chemically reasonable, while substrate-specific cyclization, decarboxylation and hydrolysis performance remain untested. The main environmental gap is achieving and maintaining the required concentrations and long staged processing, not the order or number of settings.
suggestions: Directly test alpha-ketoisovalerate and identify 5-isopropylhydantoin and N-carbamoylvaline using orthogonal analytical methods.
Track carbon incorporation and decarboxylation rather than inferring the mechanism from the balanced net equation.

Specify or experimentally relax the reference conditions of approximately 0.35 M ketoacid, concentrated cyanide/ammonia, 0.5 M bicarbonate, 21 days near room temperature and 14 days at 80 degrees Celsius; justify any required concentration process.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Huber and Wachtershauser (2003) provide experimental precedent for ferrous-hydroxide-mediated reductive amination, but not for the valine substrate. The balanced two-iron oxidation supplies an appropriate formal reducing-equivalent inventory without requiring molecular oxygen. Nevertheless, alpha-ketoisovalerate conversion, the assumed FeOOH endpoint and effective mineral surface state are unverified. Freshness, pH, ionic strength and temperature materially affect the cited chemistry, so a generic hydrothermal designation is insufficient.
suggestions: Test alpha-ketoisovalerate with freshly precipitated Fe(OH)2 while controlling pH, ionic strength, temperature and mineral aging.
Use the cited pH range near 8.8-9.3 as a starting point rather than assuming unrestricted hydrothermal compatibility.
Measure iron oxidation states and solid products, and quantify valine against competing reduction and decomposition products.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Wang et al. (2012) support ZnS-mediated photochemical amination of other alpha-ketoacids, not alpha-ketoisovalerate. Sulfite oxidation can supply the formal reducing equivalents, and the supplied check establishes conservation without an oxygen requirement. However, valine formation, selectivity, photostability and sulfate production have not been demonstrated for this substrate. An illuminated anoxic surface setting is plausible in principle, but light spectrum, photon flux, catalyst state and solution conditions are missing.
suggestions: Specify ZnS identity and loading, UV spectrum and flux, pH near the cited value of 9, reactant concentrations and oxygen exclusion.
Test alpha-ketoisovalerate directly with dark, catalyst-free and sulfite-free controls and isotope-confirmed valine identification.
Quantify sulfate and other sulfur products together with amino-acid, hydroxy-acid and photodecomposition products.

evaluation.network_feedback: The network has sufficient nodes, consistent molecule IDs and no isolated subgraphs. All 17 reactions are accepted as atom/charge conserving under the supplied deterministic check; five require explicit coefficients. The unparsable mol_018 InChI is a metadata defect, not a conservation violation, because its stated CO2 formula was checked. Formal balancing does not establish empirical product stoichiometry, particularly for rxn_006 and rxn_007. The network contains a well-supported productive core in rxn_009-rxn_011 and correctly represents rxn_012 as a competing sink; its scores under P5-P7 refer to that side branch, not additional productive steps. Imported alpha-ketoisovalerate is a legitimate starting material, and its unestablished simpler-feedstock origin limits claim scope rather than invalidating these conversions. Whole-network confidence is constrained by the unquantified branched-aldehyde output of rxn_001, unresolved empirical closures, weak modern validation of rxn_007, and untested valine-specific extensions in rxn_013, rxn_016 and rxn_017. Evidence grading aligns substantially with the supplied literature, but reaction-level citations and the thermal-route contamination caveat should be added. Separate environments and catalyst variants are acceptable and receive no numerical bonus or penalty. Environmental confidence is reduced by missing operating parameters and catalyst-state details; transfers need justification only where actually required. P6 is the strongest demonstrated conversion from its declared precursor, not a demonstrated natural end-to-end synthesis. The complete network does not meet the 0.90 approval threshold.
